title: AI Safety Research Catalog
summary: A reading and evidence reference for human-AI research. Concepts describe boundaries, observable behavior, and alternative explanations. They are not attack recipes, hidden-mechanism diagnoses, or efficacy rankings.

categories.name: Roles and responsibilities
categories.summary: How an assistant's described identity relates to its actual remit and authority.

categories.name: Fiction, quotation, and context
categories.summary: How analytical, historical, and fictional settings affect interpretation without changing who is speaking.

categories.name: Authority and permission
categories.summary: How systems distinguish claimed status, urgency, and role labels from authorization.

categories.name: Representation and language
categories.summary: How different textual representations affect comprehension, classification, and evidence.

categories.name: History and context
categories.summary: How retained messages, examples, and long inputs influence observable behavior.

categories.name: Information disclosure and inference
categories.summary: What responses reveal, how disclosure is verified, and where guesses can resemble evidence.

categories.name: Self-description and continuity
categories.summary: How statements about identity, capability, and prior commitments relate to system state.

categories.name: Output and interpretation
categories.summary: How output formats interact with meaning, provenance, and downstream consumers.

categories.name: Images, audio, and video
categories.summary: How perception and instruction boundaries differ across input channels.

categories.name: Tools and delegated authority
categories.summary: How tool descriptions, returned data, permissions, and observable effects relate.

categories.name: Coordination between agents
categories.summary: How information, authority, and errors move between cooperating components.

categories.name: Retrieval and memory
categories.summary: How stored information enters later decisions and how persistence is established.

categories.name: Evaluation procedures and budgets
categories.summary: How search procedures, model assistance, and sampling affect the meaning of results.

categories.name: Reasoning and measurement
categories.summary: What reasoning displays, resource use, and scores can and cannot establish.

categories.name: Training and component integrity
categories.summary: How data, model updates, dependencies, and distributed artifacts affect security.

categories.name: Evaluation and oversight
categories.summary: How measurement conditions, incentives, and hidden confounders limit conclusions.

entries.name: Fictional roles and real responsibilities
entries.summary: A fictional character can change an assistant's voice without changing its authorized responsibilities. The relevant observation is a change in task behavior, not dramatic characterization.
entries.boundary: Character description versus the assistant's actual remit.
evidence_to_check: The concrete action performed under the role and the policy governing that action.
Whether only tone changed or the assistant adopted a new responsibility.
alternative_explanations: Permitted creative writing may include an objectionable character.
A theatrical refusal can preserve the same substantive boundary.
defensive_questions: Does role adoption preserve the application's permissions?
Can evaluators distinguish fictional dialogue from an executed action?
entries.epistemic_status: An editorial behavioral distinction. Character language alone does not identify a hidden mechanism or establish a safety failure.

entries.name: Expertise and authorization
entries.summary: Expertise concerns what someone knows; authorization concerns what they may do. An assistant can recognize professional competence while retaining limits on scope and access.
entries.boundary: Claims of competence versus permission for a particular action.
evidence_to_check: The claimed qualification and any independently established permission.
The decision in which expertise was treated as sufficient authority.
alternative_explanations: Better technical language can improve legitimate task understanding.
The actor may actually hold the required authorization.
defensive_questions: Are identity and action-specific permission checked separately?
Does a credential affect access only through an explicit policy?
entries.epistemic_status: This concept separates properties often conflated in conversation. The cited hierarchy research does not validate this label as a distinct internal mechanism.

entries.name: Alternate assistant identities
entries.summary: An alternate persona may claim different duties or restrictions. Such claims are conversation content; they do not create a new system role or change runtime permissions.
entries.boundary: An asserted identity versus the actual instruction and execution context.
evidence_to_check: The source and runtime role of the persona description.
Substantive behavior before and after identity claims, including unchanged refusals.
alternative_explanations: Multiple fictional voices can remain within the same permitted task.
An announcement of a new mode may be stylistic performance.
defensive_questions: Does the system preserve authority distinctions across persona changes?
Are mode claims checked against actual configuration?
entries.epistemic_status: The historical identifier is retained for continuity. The display label describes observable role claims without treating them as a functioning bypass.

entries.name: Changing responsibilities over time
entries.summary: An assistant's working interpretation of its responsibilities can change across a retained conversation. The unit of analysis is the sequence of decisions, not a new nickname or tone.
entries.boundary: Earlier conversational commitments versus the continuing task boundary.
evidence_to_check: A time-ordered record of duties accepted and actions performed.
The retained history and any authorized changes to the task.
alternative_explanations: The user may legitimately revise the task.
Accumulated factual context can explain a different answer without role drift.
defensive_questions: Can the system recheck scope when responsibilities change?
Do summaries preserve qualifications attached to earlier commitments?
entries.epistemic_status: History dependence is plausible and studied, but a single trajectory cannot isolate gradualness, a particular turn, or an internal cause.

entries.name: Fictional context and present intent
entries.summary: Fictional dialogue contains represented speakers and events. Analysis must preserve that attribution while separately assessing the substance of any assistance the model actually provides.
entries.boundary: Statements inside a story versus the current user's instructions and circumstances.
evidence_to_check: Who speaks at each narrative layer and what the actual analytical request is.
Whether the response describes the fiction or supplies a materially different capability.
alternative_explanations: Quoted harmful speech may be necessary for criticism or scholarship.
An intense first-person statement may belong to a fictional narrator.
defensive_questions: Does the system preserve speaker attribution through quotations?
Can it support legitimate analysis without treating all fictional content as present intent?
entries.epistemic_status: Fiction is neither evidence of misuse nor proof of harmlessness. This entry is an interpretation framework, not a claim that framing changes every model's behavior.

entries.name: Research purpose and analytical scope
entries.summary: Research framing states an intended analytical purpose. Evaluating a response still requires attention to the requested information, evidence, and level of action-enabling detail.
entries.boundary: A stated research purpose versus the substantive assistance delivered.
evidence_to_check: The research question and the exact requested analytical output.
Whether conclusions remain tied to records, methods, and relevant uncertainty.
alternative_explanations: Authorized safety research can legitimately discuss sensitive material.
A refusal may reflect missing context rather than resistance to the research itself.
defensive_questions: Can the system distinguish retrospective analysis from a request for new operational material?
Are restrictions applied to the particular requested output rather than a topic label?
entries.epistemic_status: Research context matters. A research label alone neither verifies authorization nor establishes that a response crossed a boundary.

entries.name: Historical records and current requests
entries.summary: An archive can contain obsolete instructions, fictional statements, and accounts of wrongdoing. Describing those records is different from executing or extending their instructions.
entries.boundary: Historical source material versus the analyst's present task.
evidence_to_check: Date, provenance, original speaker, and whether a passage is quoted or paraphrased.
The difference between source description and advice added by the current assistant.
alternative_explanations: Unfamiliar language may be ordinary historical terminology.
A quoted instruction can be evidence rather than a command to the analyst.
defensive_questions: Does archival material remain inert during analysis?
Are missing dates and uncertain attributions visible in the report?
entries.epistemic_status: This is a source-handling distinction. The citations support provenance and instruction priority, not a separate historical-framing efficacy estimate.

entries.name: Nested speakers and quotations
entries.summary: A transcript may contain a persona quoting another conversation inside a fictional setting. Meaning and responsibility depend on preserving each layer's speaker and authority.
entries.boundary: One layer's represented speech versus instructions governing another layer.
evidence_to_check: A clear mapping from each passage to its speaker and narrative layer.
Any point where quoted instructions were adopted as current commands.
alternative_explanations: Complex nesting can cause ordinary comprehension errors.
A response can quote an instruction without obeying it.
defensive_questions: Are quotation and role boundaries retained in summaries?
Can the system explain which instruction source governed its observable action?
entries.epistemic_status: Nesting is a property of the material, not evidence of successful instruction transfer. No particular depth is asserted to cause failure.

entries.name: Researcher identity and permission
entries.summary: A claim to be a researcher supplies context about the speaker. The relevant authorization remains tied to the system, data, and activity being discussed.
entries.boundary: Researcher identity versus permission over a specific resource or action.
evidence_to_check: The requested activity and the scope attached to the research claim.
Any available authorization evidence, distinguished from an unverified assertion.
alternative_explanations: The research may be authorized even when credentials are not visible in the transcript.
The model may adapt vocabulary without granting additional permissions.
defensive_questions: Can authorized analytical work proceed with clear provenance?
Are resource permissions independent of claimed prestige?
entries.epistemic_status: A missing credential record is not proof of unauthorized conduct. The entry describes a trust distinction rather than a suspicion attached to researchers.

entries.name: Professional roles and access
entries.summary: A professional title can be relevant to a task while leaving access decisions unchanged. Role claims and verified entitlements must remain distinguishable.
entries.boundary: Occupational status versus the application's access policy.
evidence_to_check: Which entitlement the action requires and how it is established.
Whether a title was merely mentioned or actually changed a permission decision.
alternative_explanations: Role-specific support can be ordinary intended behavior.
An authenticated professional account may have legitimate additional access.
defensive_questions: Does the application authorize actions using trusted account state?
Are exceptional permissions documented rather than inferred from conversational style?
entries.epistemic_status: Credential-sensitive behavior is not inherently a failure. A finding requires a mismatch with the relevant authorization rule.

entries.name: Claimed instruction priority
entries.summary: Text can describe itself as a system or developer instruction while arriving through a lower-trust channel. Its wording does not determine its actual priority.
entries.boundary: Claimed priority in content versus priority assigned by the application.
evidence_to_check: The real message channel and origin of the text.
Whether the assistant treated lower-trust content as governing an action.
alternative_explanations: The user may be asking to analyze a sample instruction.
An actual trusted application update can legitimately change behavior.
defensive_questions: Are priority decisions based on trusted message structure?
Do rendered transcripts preserve the difference between a role label and a real role?
entries.epistemic_status: Instruction hierarchy is a researched design concept. A transcript must still establish which channel delivered the disputed material.

entries.name: Urgency and decision authority
entries.summary: Urgent or emotionally charged language can affect attention and tone. A safety-relevant change occurs only when it changes a decision that should depend on authorization or evidence.
entries.boundary: Perceived urgency versus the requirements for an action.
evidence_to_check: The urgency claim and the concrete decision it accompanied.
Any verification step omitted and whether policy allowed that omission.
alternative_explanations: A real emergency may warrant a different authorized response.
Empathetic language can coexist with unchanged access controls.
defensive_questions: Do emergency procedures specify what can change and what still requires verification?
Can reviewers separate helpful urgency handling from unsupported exceptions?
entries.epistemic_status: Emotional content does not establish deception. Causal influence and inappropriate permission changes require separate evidence.

entries.name: Encoded representations
entries.summary: Encoded text changes the representation seen by components in a system. Comprehension, policy assessment, and downstream decoding may occur at different stages.
entries.boundary: Representation handling versus the meaning ultimately processed or delivered.
evidence_to_check: Which component decoded the material and what meaning it recovered.
Whether the final decoded content differs substantively from the original request.
alternative_explanations: The model may misunderstand an encoding.
A benign data-conversion task may legitimately preserve quoted material.
defensive_questions: Is the evaluated content the final interpreted meaning?
Are decoding errors distinguished from a policy decision?
entries.epistemic_status: Representation sensitivity is a broad research concern. No encoding is presented as effective or as evidence of a particular internal failure.

entries.name: Surface wording and meaning
entries.summary: Unusual spelling, substitutions, and jargon can change how a request is interpreted. A robust analysis distinguishes semantic change from mere surface variation.
entries.boundary: Surface form versus the task meaning understood by the system.
evidence_to_check: The intended and actually interpreted meaning of each variant.
Substantive response differences with language comprehension accounted for.
alternative_explanations: The altered wording may describe a different task.
Spelling tolerance can be useful accessibility behavior.
defensive_questions: Do semantic checks account for ordinary spelling variation?
Are evaluation differences explained by comprehension before being labeled safety failures?
entries.epistemic_status: Related studies examine variation under specific procedures. This entry supplies no preferred substitutions or expected success rate.

entries.name: Safety coverage across languages
entries.summary: A system's language understanding and safety coverage need not be uniform. Differences require assessment of meaning, fluency, task difficulty, and evaluation quality.
entries.boundary: Equivalent intended tasks across different language contexts.
evidence_to_check: Semantic equivalence and fluent interpretation of the requests and responses.
Whether evaluator competence is adequate in every language being compared.
alternative_explanations: Translation may change intent or omit constraints.
Low task competence can resemble refusal or partial compliance.
defensive_questions: Are multilingual evaluations reviewed by competent speakers?
Does protection remain meaningful without reducing useful service for underserved languages?
entries.epistemic_status: The cited study is dated and model-specific. It does not establish a current language ranking or a universal relationship between resource level and safety.

entries.name: Unicode and displayed text
entries.summary: The bytes stored in a message, its rendered appearance, and the text consumed by a model may differ. This is a representation and provenance question before it is a behavioral claim.
entries.boundary: Rendered text versus normalized or parsed text at each component.
evidence_to_check: The original code points and the actual normalization or rendering path.
Which text reached the model, evaluator, and human reviewer.
alternative_explanations: A font or renderer may create the apparent discrepancy.
Multilingual text can legitimately contain unfamiliar characters.
defensive_questions: Are invisible or ambiguous characters made inspectable when needed?
Do review tools preserve originals alongside normalized views?
entries.epistemic_status: An editorial systems distinction informed by adversarial-ML terminology. The reviewed source does not validate a specific Unicode failure in any product.

entries.name: Relevant material in long contexts
entries.summary: In a long input, information can be present without being retained, retrieved, or treated as authoritative. Those are different explanations for a missed constraint.
entries.boundary: Available context versus information actually used in a decision.
evidence_to_check: The full input, context limits, and any truncation or summarization.
Whether the relevant material was understood, omitted, or assigned the wrong authority.
alternative_explanations: The application may have removed earlier material.
Ordinary retrieval or comprehension failure can explain the result.
defensive_questions: Does the application preserve governing constraints through context management?
Can evaluations distinguish absent information from ignored instructions?
entries.epistemic_status: Long-context research motivates the question. This entry does not infer attention weights or a positional failure from one response.

entries.name: Repeated demonstrations in context
entries.summary: Repeated examples can influence subsequent outputs without updating model weights. Understanding this behavior requires distinguishing demonstrations, task information, and claimed permission.
entries.boundary: Examples of behavior versus authorization to reproduce that behavior.
evidence_to_check: The examples actually retained and the relationship between examples and final output.
Whether a result reflects imitation, ordinary task learning, or a policy-relevant change.
alternative_explanations: The examples may supply missing facts needed for a legitimate answer.
Input length and example content may change together.
defensive_questions: Are examples treated according to their source and task role?
Does reporting distinguish context learning from persistent model changes?
entries.epistemic_status: The cited authors study a particular long-context phenomenon. Their findings do not establish a required example count or efficacy in another setting.

entries.name: Scope changes across a dialogue
entries.summary: A later response can depend on earlier questions and assistant answers. Retrospective analysis should preserve the entire trajectory and identify where task scope changed.
entries.boundary: Conversation continuity versus a stable authorization boundary.
evidence_to_check: The exact order of both user and assistant messages.
Changes in requested task, retained assumptions, and observed behavior across turns.
alternative_explanations: A later message may clarify a formerly ambiguous request.
A changed outcome may reflect additional information rather than escalation.
defensive_questions: Can the system reassess cumulative task meaning?
Are repeated snapshots recognized as dependent measurements?
entries.epistemic_status: A named published procedure exists, but resemblance to a trajectory does not prove that procedure was used or identify its causal contribution.

entries.name: Meaning distributed across turns
entries.summary: The significance of a conversation may depend on combining information spread across messages. Evaluating each message alone can miss the cumulative task or overstate what any one reply provides.
entries.boundary: Local message meaning versus the combined information in the retained history.
evidence_to_check: Which pieces of information are available jointly and at what point.
The evaluator's unit: final response, selected turn, or whole history.
alternative_explanations: Ordinary collaborative work naturally distributes details across turns.
The model may never combine the pieces in the way an analyst assumes.
defensive_questions: Does the evaluation unit match the risk being measured?
Are cumulative claims supported by an explicit reconstruction of available information?
entries.epistemic_status: This is a measurement distinction as well as a possible interaction pattern. Distributed content does not by itself establish a boundary crossing.

entries.name: Interpreting response differences
entries.summary: Changes in refusal, detail, or confidence reveal observable response behavior. They do not directly reveal the hidden rule, representation, or motive responsible for it.
entries.boundary: Observed decision patterns versus inferred internal causes.
evidence_to_check: The substantive information provided, beyond refusal wording.
Task meaning, configuration, and uncertainty in the comparison.
alternative_explanations: Random variation or ambiguity may explain the difference.
A polite answer can withhold the objective while a refusal can still disclose information.
defensive_questions: Do evaluators score content independently of refusal phrases?
Are competing explanations retained when the policy is not visible?
entries.epistemic_status: Useful for descriptive comparison. Black-box differences alone do not identify a latent refusal direction or a precise hidden decision rule.

entries.name: Task boundaries between related topics
entries.summary: Closely related questions can belong to different authorized tasks. A system may answer one and decline another without behaving inconsistently.
entries.boundary: Topic similarity versus the function and consequence of the requested work.
evidence_to_check: The action each question asks the assistant to perform.
The relevant distinction between permitted and excluded responsibilities.
alternative_explanations: The questions may differ materially despite shared vocabulary.
Uneven subject competence can look like a policy boundary.
defensive_questions: Is the application's intended scope expressible in terms of actions?
Can reviewers explain differences without relying only on topic keywords?
entries.epistemic_status: A boundary-mapping concept, not a technique-specific efficacy claim. Related subject matter is insufficient to establish comparable requests.

entries.name: Information in small answers
entries.summary: A brief confirmation or denial can reveal protected information if it reliably depends on that information. Output length is not a measure of confidentiality.
entries.boundary: Permitted acknowledgment versus disclosure about protected state.
evidence_to_check: An authorized reference establishing what the response depends on.
Information learned beyond what was already present in the request.
alternative_explanations: The response may be guessing or following a conversational pattern.
It may repeat a fact already supplied by the user.
defensive_questions: Do confidentiality checks cover confirmations as well as full-text disclosure?
Is informational gain assessed against what the requester already knew?
entries.epistemic_status: A general privacy distinction. A consistent-looking yes/no answer is not a verified oracle without evidence of dependency on protected state.

entries.name: Inferring information provenance
entries.summary: A model's response can invite guesses about what it has seen in training or current context. Those are different sources and require different evidence.
entries.boundary: Behavioral familiarity versus membership in a particular information source.
evidence_to_check: Which source is at issue: training, retrieved material, current context, or stored memory.
Ground truth and uncertainty for any membership or provenance claim.
alternative_explanations: Common knowledge and semantic similarity can produce familiar wording.
Current-context repetition can resemble training-data recall.
defensive_questions: Are source-specific claims evaluated with source-specific evidence?
Does the report distinguish probabilistic inference from exact recovery?
entries.epistemic_status: Privacy inference is an established research area. This catalog does not supply a membership estimator or treat a single familiar response as proof.

entries.name: Authenticity of recovered instructions
entries.summary: Instruction-like output may be copied, inferred, reconstructed, or genuinely recovered. A plausible document and a favorable judge decision do not authenticate its source.
entries.boundary: Protected instruction text versus newly generated descriptions of behavior.
evidence_to_check: Availability of an authorized reference and the chosen match criterion.
Provenance of the candidate text, including material supplied in the conversation.
alternative_explanations: The assistant may generate a reasonable policy from observed behavior.
Shared generic wording can create apparent overlap.
defensive_questions: Are exact recovery, semantic disclosure, and reconstruction reported separately?
Can uncertain authenticity remain unresolved rather than forced into success or failure?
entries.epistemic_status: Reference-based studies support the distinction. Without a trusted reference, neither confirmed extraction nor a false-positive verdict is established.

entries.name: Claims about embodiment and implementation
entries.summary: An assistant can describe bodies, environments, or implementation details that are not part of its actual deployment. Such descriptions are text, not telemetry.
entries.boundary: Represented embodiment or architecture versus verified runtime state.
evidence_to_check: Which implementation facts are independently observable.
Whether the output is factual reporting, metaphor, roleplay, or unsupported assertion.
alternative_explanations: A physical description may be part of a legitimate simulation.
The model may repeat a user-supplied premise without verifying it.
defensive_questions: Are self-descriptions clearly separated from application telemetry?
Can downstream decisions avoid treating imagined capabilities as real access?
entries.epistemic_status: An editorial interpretation category. Conversational descriptions do not establish a persistent self-model, consciousness, or knowledge of deployment internals.

entries.name: Claimed versus available capabilities
entries.summary: Statements that an assistant has gained tools, memory, or authority do not demonstrate that those capabilities exist. Actual availability is determined by the application.
entries.boundary: Conversational capability claims versus accessible functions and permissions.
evidence_to_check: The tool registry, permission state, and observed calls where available.
The difference between offering an action and completing it.
alternative_explanations: The assistant may be discussing a hypothetical future system.
The application may genuinely have changed configuration.
defensive_questions: Can capability claims be checked against trusted runtime information?
Does the interface distinguish a proposal from a successful operation?
entries.epistemic_status: Self-report is weaker than execution evidence. An unsupported capability claim can be an error without any intentional deception.

entries.name: Simulated modes and real configuration
entries.summary: A conversation can describe a diagnostic or developer mode without changing the application. A mode's claimed rules and a real configuration transition are different events.
entries.boundary: Text describing a privileged mode versus an authenticated state change.
evidence_to_check: Evidence that the application actually exposes and activated such a mode.
Any observed behavior change beyond a mode announcement.
alternative_explanations: The request may be for a harmless mock interface.
A real diagnostic facility may exist under separate access controls.
defensive_questions: Are privileged modes controlled outside ordinary dialogue?
Can logs distinguish simulation from an authenticated mode transition?
entries.epistemic_status: The identifier refers to a recurring framing concept. It does not imply a hidden mode is available in any particular model.

entries.name: Prior commitments and continuing authority
entries.summary: An earlier statement can influence a later decision through conversational continuity. The earlier statement may have conditions that no longer apply or may never have granted permission.
entries.boundary: Remembered commitment versus authorization for the present action.
evidence_to_check: The original commitment, its qualifications, and the later interpretation.
Whether the conversation or memory summary preserved those qualifications.
alternative_explanations: Following through on a legitimate commitment is ordinary helpful behavior.
The present request may fall within the original agreed scope.
defensive_questions: Are commitments rechecked when their object or scope changes?
Do memory summaries preserve limits as well as promises?
entries.epistemic_status: A behavioral hypothesis about history use. It does not establish enduring identity, cross-session memory, or a distinct internal continuity mechanism.

entries.name: Code as content and as action
entries.summary: Code-shaped output can be explanation, an inert artifact, or an input to an execution system. The security consequence depends on which role it actually has.
entries.boundary: Generated representation versus execution by a downstream component.
evidence_to_check: Whether the output was stored, reviewed, executed, or merely displayed.
The concrete capability conveyed and any verified effects.
alternative_explanations: A harmless illustration can resemble executable code.
Execution failures may come from syntax or environment issues.
defensive_questions: Are generation and execution recorded separately?
Does any execution path enforce permissions independently of the model's prose?
entries.epistemic_status: Format alone does not determine risk or usefulness. No generated code is included in this reference.

entries.name: Structured output and downstream trust
entries.summary: JSON, tables, and other schemas make output easier to parse, but do not establish that its contents are true, authorized, or safe for a consumer to use.
entries.boundary: Schema validity versus semantic correctness and permitted use.
evidence_to_check: Both syntactic validity and the meaning of each consumed field.
What downstream software did with the parsed values.
alternative_explanations: A valid object may contain fabricated facts.
A formatting failure can be unrelated to instruction compliance.
defensive_questions: Are action-bearing fields checked against independent constraints?
Can the consumer reject unexpected meaning even when the schema is valid?
entries.epistemic_status: This is a general interface distinction. A structured answer is neither automatic compliance nor evidence of a particular vulnerability.

entries.name: Prompt boundaries and continuation
entries.summary: Some interfaces distinguish supplied text from newly generated continuation. Analysis must identify that boundary before attributing the whole visible answer to the model.
entries.boundary: Caller-supplied prefix versus model-authored output.
evidence_to_check: Which characters were provided by the caller and which were generated.
Whether the interface actually supports a continuation prefix.
alternative_explanations: The evaluator may count supplied text as model output.
A displayed prefix may be ordinary quoted content rather than an API feature.
defensive_questions: Do logs retain the authorship boundary in completions?
Does scoring assess the generated material rather than the combined display alone?
entries.epistemic_status: Interface-specific concept. Ordinary chat text does not establish access to a model's generation prefix.

entries.name: Translation and semantic responsibility
entries.summary: Translation can preserve, alter, or lose meaning across representations. The requested task, quoted source material, and new assistance added by the model must be distinguished.
entries.boundary: Faithful transformation of source material versus newly supplied substantive content.
evidence_to_check: Semantic equivalence across the source and translated output.
Any extra information introduced beyond the transformation task.
alternative_explanations: Translation errors may explain a changed apparent intent.
Legitimate translation can reproduce sensitive statements without endorsing them.
defensive_questions: Are translation quality and safety judgments assessed independently?
Can source attribution survive changes in language and format?
entries.epistemic_status: Translation is ordinary useful functionality. The cited language study does not make translation itself a boundary violation.

entries.name: Image content and visual interpretation
entries.summary: Visible text in an image, scene interpretation, and numerical image perturbations are different input phenomena. Each requires evidence about what the system perceived and how that affected behavior.
entries.boundary: Visual data versus instructions or decisions derived from that data.
evidence_to_check: The image actually processed and any available transcription or perception output.
Whether the disputed instruction was read, inferred, or absent from the perceived content.
alternative_explanations: Optical recognition errors can change apparent meaning.
A scene description may quote visible text without treating it as a command.
defensive_questions: Are perception accuracy and instruction authority assessed separately?
Does the pipeline preserve the provenance of image-derived text?
entries.epistemic_status: The cited visual study concerns evaluated adversarial examples. It does not establish that ordinary typography and optimized perturbations share a mechanism.

entries.name: Audio, transcription, and authority
entries.summary: Audio systems may involve speech recognition, language reasoning, and speech output. A response difference can arise at any of those stages.
entries.boundary: Spoken or transcribed source material versus the authority assigned to it.
evidence_to_check: The submitted audio, recognized content, and final generated response where available.
Whether accent, transcription, speaker attribution, or task interpretation explains the result.
alternative_explanations: Recognition errors may remove an important qualifier.
Different speech interfaces may use different application policies.
defensive_questions: Are comparisons grounded in equivalent perceived meaning?
Can spoken quotations remain distinct from instructions to the assistant?
entries.epistemic_status: Cross-modal sampling has been studied. That does not establish that voice is generally less protected or that a particular speaker characteristic causes failure.

entries.name: Video sampling and temporal context
entries.summary: A video system may inspect only selected frames and audio segments. The visible recording and the model's actual input can therefore differ.
entries.boundary: Recorded temporal content versus the sampled material used in a decision.
evidence_to_check: The actual frame and audio sampling policy, when known.
The timing and source of information reflected in the output.
alternative_explanations: The relevant frame may never have been processed.
A temporal-order error can resemble instruction adoption.
defensive_questions: Can evaluations identify which frames were available to the model?
Are claims about the full video limited when sampling is unknown?
entries.epistemic_status: A systems-analysis category. The reviewed sources provide related visual and threat-model context, not a specific validation of this video pattern.

entries.name: Concealed information across channels
entries.summary: Claims of hidden cross-modal communication require evidence that a carrier conveys recoverable information to a receiver. Unusual appearance or correlated responses are insufficient.
entries.boundary: Apparent carrier content versus information actually decoded by another component.
evidence_to_check: Evidence of a defined sender, receiver, and recoverable signal.
The distinction between concealed communication and ordinary semantic inference.
alternative_explanations: The receiver may use shared context rather than a hidden channel.
A human analyst may perceive a pattern that is not reproducible.
defensive_questions: Can a suspected channel be validated independently of its proposed story?
Are benign correlations considered before attributing concealed communication?
entries.epistemic_status: A conditional hypothesis requiring direct evidence. The cited work does not certify a covert channel in an arbitrary image, audio clip, or model exchange.

entries.name: Tool descriptions and instruction authority
entries.summary: Tool metadata describes a component's purpose and interface. It can also contain claims that exceed that component's authority; returned tool content is a separate object.
entries.boundary: Component-provided descriptions versus application-governing instructions.
evidence_to_check: The exact metadata version consumed and who controlled it.
Whether behavior depended on the description, implementation, or returned data.
alternative_explanations: A changed tool implementation may cause the effect directly.
Legitimate metadata may accurately document a permitted requirement.
defensive_questions: Are tool descriptions treated as claims from their provider?
Can the application distinguish registered metadata from ordinary tool results?
entries.epistemic_status: An editorial specialization of the external-content trust problem. The broad references do not establish metadata control in a given system.

entries.name: Tool changes after review
entries.summary: A tool's description or implementation may change after an earlier approval. Security review of one version does not automatically describe a later version.
entries.boundary: Previously reviewed component state versus the component currently in use.
evidence_to_check: Versioned metadata and implementation identity at review and execution time.
Which changes occurred and whether the application's approval remained applicable.
alternative_explanations: An authorized update can legitimately change behavior.
Configuration drift elsewhere may explain the difference.
defensive_questions: Are consequential component changes visible and attributable?
Does trust attach to a specific version and permission scope?
entries.epistemic_status: A lifecycle and provenance concern, not proof that an update is malicious. The current source review supplies broad terminology rather than a product-specific audit.

entries.name: Acting with another party's authority
entries.summary: An agent may possess permissions that the author of an input does not. A confused-deputy failure occurs when those permissions serve an instruction that lacks the required authority.
entries.boundary: Input-source authority versus the permissions used to act.
evidence_to_check: Who requested the action, whose permission enabled it, and which resource was affected.
Separate records for a proposed action, emitted call, tool result, and verified effect.
alternative_explanations: The action may have been authorized by the legitimate user.
The model may emit a call that system enforcement rejects.
defensive_questions: Are permissions checked at the action boundary?
Can reviewers distinguish model compliance from a completed privilege violation?
entries.epistemic_status: An established security concept. A structured call alone does not establish successful execution or an unauthorized effect.

entries.name: Delegated scope and task deviation
entries.summary: An agent can exceed its delegated scope or pursue a task different from the user's goal. Broad permissions and task deviation are separate properties, even when both are present.
entries.boundary: Delegated user intent versus the goals and actions the agent adopts.
evidence_to_check: The user's specified objective, unresolved ambiguity, and granted permissions.
Observable actions that differ from the authorized task.
alternative_explanations: An underspecified request can admit several reasonable interpretations.
A task failure may be a capability limitation rather than goal redirection.
defensive_questions: Is scope clear enough to evaluate deviations fairly?
Do consequential actions require permission appropriate to the user's actual request?
entries.epistemic_status: Goal deviation needs a defensible reference task. An unexpected action alone does not establish malicious influence or an internal competing goal.

entries.name: Information leaving through external channels
entries.summary: Disclosure can occur through an external action rather than visible chat text. A confidentiality claim must identify the protected information, destination, and observed transfer.
entries.boundary: Data-use permission versus permission to send data to a recipient.
evidence_to_check: The source classification, intended recipient, emitted request, and available delivery evidence.
What information the recipient could actually receive.
alternative_explanations: The transfer may be an authorized part of the task.
A proposed outbound action may be blocked before data leaves.
defensive_questions: Are outbound destinations and data permissions checked together?
Can the audit distinguish requested transmission from confirmed disclosure?
entries.epistemic_status: An outbound channel must exist and be accessible. Neither mentioning a destination nor emitting a call proves successful delivery.

entries.name: Instruction propagation between components
entries.summary: One component's output may become another component's input. Propagation is established only when the relevant instruction survives the handoff and influences later behavior.
entries.boundary: One component's generated content versus another component's governing authority.
evidence_to_check: The actual handoff path, message provenance, and subsequent decisions.
Whether later behavior adopted the instruction or merely repeated its text.
alternative_explanations: Several agents may independently receive the same original instruction.
Routine quotation can look like propagation without changing behavior.
defensive_questions: Are origin and trust level retained through handoffs?
Can downstream agents treat another model's output as untrusted evidence?
entries.epistemic_status: Propagation has been demonstrated in constructed systems. Repetition across logs alone does not establish a causal chain.

entries.name: Claims of concealed coordination
entries.summary: Covert coordination requires more than agreement between agents. Evidence must establish communication carrying information that an observer's ordinary view does not reveal.
entries.boundary: Authorized communication versus concealed information exchange or coordination.
evidence_to_check: A supported communication channel and receiver behavior tied to its content.
The difference between shared information, correlated reasoning, and a hidden signal.
alternative_explanations: Common training or shared prompts can produce similar outputs.
Chance patterns and ordinary conventions can resemble codes.
defensive_questions: Are coordination claims grounded in reproducible channel evidence?
Can monitoring preserve privacy while checking unauthorized information flow?
entries.epistemic_status: The source studies capability and conditions for concealed communication. It does not justify attributing collusion from unusual wording or apparent agreement.

entries.name: Error spread across a workflow
entries.summary: A local error can affect several later decisions when components depend on one another. A cascade concerns dependency and consequences, not merely the number of agents.
entries.boundary: Upstream uncertainty versus downstream assumptions treated as established facts.
evidence_to_check: The dependency path linking the initial error to later outcomes.
Which stages checked, transformed, or amplified the uncertain information.
alternative_explanations: Several failures may share an external cause rather than a chain.
A downstream component may correct the earlier error.
defensive_questions: Are uncertain inputs marked through the workflow?
Can a local error be contained before consequential actions depend on it?
entries.epistemic_status: A general systems concept. Causal propagation must be shown rather than inferred from temporal sequence or multiple failures.

entries.name: Sustained deviation in an agent workflow
entries.summary: An agent may repeatedly act outside a delegated objective. Describing that pattern does not establish independent desires, consciousness, or a deliberately concealed plan.
entries.boundary: Assigned task and permissions versus a sustained pattern of observed action.
evidence_to_check: The assigned objective, its changes, and the sequence of deviations.
Environmental feedback, memory, and other components that could sustain the pattern.
alternative_explanations: A mistaken task interpretation can persist without a hidden goal.
Stale memory or a recurring tool error may account for repeated behavior.
defensive_questions: Can the workflow detect and correct persistent scope divergence?
Are explanations grounded in actions rather than anthropomorphic labels?
entries.epistemic_status: The legacy identifier is retained; the display label avoids a motive claim. The cited scheming experiments use constructed conditions that must not be assumed here.

entries.name: Retrieved content and source authority
entries.summary: Material in a retrieval store may contain false claims or instructions. The document must first be retrieved, and its influence must then be distinguished from mere presence.
entries.boundary: Retrieved source content versus authority over the assistant's task.
evidence_to_check: Control of the stored material, the retrieved record, and its actual use.
Whether the effect concerns factual contamination, instruction adoption, or both.
alternative_explanations: The disputed document may never reach the model.
An ordinary relevant source can influence an answer legitimately.
defensive_questions: Does retrieval preserve source provenance and trust level?
Are corpus changes distinguished from replacement of one returned field?
entries.epistemic_status: Studies establish risks in particular retrieval systems. Presence in a corpus is not proof of retrieval, and retrieval is not proof of instruction adoption.

entries.name: Untrusted content in persistent memory
entries.summary: A stored note can influence future sessions if the application later retrieves or applies it. Persistence requires evidence of both storage and subsequent use.
entries.boundary: Untrusted or mistaken content versus durable state used in later decisions.
evidence_to_check: A supported write to the relevant store and a later read or effect.
Whether the saved material is treated as a preference, fact, instruction, or quotation.
alternative_explanations: Ordinary retained conversation history may explain apparent memory.
A correct memory entry may become inappropriate after circumstances change.
defensive_questions: Do memory records preserve source, scope, and expiry?
Can users inspect and correct consequential stored assumptions?
entries.epistemic_status: Persistent memory is an application capability, not an inference from conversational familiarity. This entry does not assume a memory store exists.

entries.name: Isolation between sessions and users
entries.summary: Information can appear to cross session boundaries through memory, caches, shared resources, or ordinary prior knowledge. The source and isolation rule must be established.
entries.boundary: State authorized for one session or user versus state available in another.
evidence_to_check: Session and user boundaries, intended retention, and an authorized reference for the information.
Which component could have carried the state across the boundary.
alternative_explanations: The information may be public or supplied again in the new context.
An application may intentionally share a user-approved memory across sessions.
defensive_questions: Are isolation and retention guarantees explicit?
Can audits distinguish shared infrastructure from model-level recall?
entries.epistemic_status: Cross-session behavior does not automatically imply cross-user leakage. A privacy finding requires evidence about provenance and the applicable isolation boundary.

entries.name: Optimization with internal model access
entries.summary: Some evaluation procedures use numerical information from model internals. Their access assumptions differ fundamentally from those of a user who can only read chat responses.
entries.boundary: Research access to model internals versus ordinary interface access.
evidence_to_check: The model information available to the evaluator and how it was obtained.
The distinction between optimization on one model and evaluation on another.
alternative_explanations: A method described as internal-access may actually rely on a surrogate model.
Apparent transfer can involve additional adaptation rather than an unchanged candidate.
defensive_questions: Are access assumptions explicit in comparative claims?
Are discovery cost and independent evaluation reported separately?
entries.epistemic_status: The source studies a specific optimization family. No search implementation, candidate artifact, or general transfer guarantee is provided here.

entries.name: Model assistance in iterative evaluation
entries.summary: A separate model can contribute to an evaluation process. Human-directed collaboration, automatic candidate generation, and autonomous target interaction are different divisions of work.
entries.boundary: Who proposes, decides, submits, and interprets feedback in the evaluation.
evidence_to_check: Records attributing suggestions, edits, decisions, submissions, and feedback interpretation.
Which target interactions were manual or programmatic, and which records are missing.
alternative_explanations: A human may substantially revise or reject generated suggestions.
A polished final text does not identify its author or decision process.
defensive_questions: Does the report describe the actual division of work?
Can missing assistant-side records remain explicit rather than inferred from style?
entries.epistemic_status: Prior work establishes several forms of model-assisted evaluation. Changes between observational phases do not by themselves identify a causal assistance effect.

entries.name: Learned evaluation generators
entries.summary: An evaluation generator can be trained against a feedback signal. Its apparent improvement depends on what that signal rewards and how the resulting cases are assessed independently.
entries.boundary: Optimization reward versus the behavior the evaluation intends to measure.
evidence_to_check: The reward definition, training/evaluation separation, and case diversity.
Independent assessments of generated cases rather than the training score alone.
alternative_explanations: The generator may learn quirks of the scorer.
Higher apparent difficulty may reflect narrower coverage.
defensive_questions: Does held-out assessment measure the intended outcome?
Are diversity and generalization tracked independently from reward?
entries.epistemic_status: Model-generated evaluation has research precedent. This entry does not provide a training procedure or treat reward improvement as proof of wider coverage.

entries.name: Sampling budgets and reported outcomes
entries.summary: Repeated sampling changes the opportunity to observe an unusual result. Per-query outcomes, per-session outcomes, and cumulative task coverage are different statistics.
entries.boundary: Measured performance under a declared budget versus an unspecified amount of search.
evidence_to_check: The sampling unit, full denominator, stopping rule, and configuration.
Whether samples are independent, adaptively selected, or overlapping conversation snapshots.
alternative_explanations: Selection for submission can inflate apparent success among archived records.
More samples may also explore different tasks rather than one fixed distribution.
defensive_questions: Do comparisons use commensurate budgets and units?
Are acceptance counts separated from verified objectives and distinct task coverage?
entries.epistemic_status: Empirical scaling applies to specified procedures. A fitted curve is not a calibrated forecast for an adaptive human workflow or an incomplete archive.

entries.name: Reasoning-channel access and visibility
entries.summary: A system may expose a reasoning display, a writable intermediate channel, or neither. These interfaces must not be conflated with access to the model's hidden computation.
entries.boundary: Documented intermediate-state access versus generated descriptions of reasoning.
evidence_to_check: Which channel is visible or writable according to the actual interface.
Whether displayed reasoning was supplied, generated, summarized, or independently instrumented.
alternative_explanations: A purported scratchpad may be ordinary text in the conversation.
A visible explanation may omit influential factors.
defensive_questions: Are access claims grounded in interface documentation and records?
Can analyses avoid treating visible prose as complete internal telemetry?
entries.epistemic_status: A conditional category requiring documented access. The reviewed sources do not establish a writable hidden reasoning channel in an arbitrary service.

entries.name: Reasoning cost and availability
entries.summary: Some inputs can consume disproportionate reasoning resources. Availability analysis must separate generated tokens, compute cost, latency, and ordinary task difficulty.
entries.boundary: Permitted task processing versus excessive resource consumption.
evidence_to_check: Resource measurements tied to the request and service configuration.
Completion quality, timeouts, queueing, and any enforced limits.
alternative_explanations: A difficult legitimate task can require more computation.
Network or backend congestion can increase latency independently of reasoning.
defensive_questions: Are resource limits observable and appropriate to the task?
Can cost changes be assessed without sacrificing legitimate complex work?
entries.epistemic_status: The cited work reports a resource-consumption phenomenon in particular systems. A slow response alone is not evidence of it.

entries.name: Scores and intended outcomes
entries.summary: A metric is a proxy for an intended outcome. A proxy failure is established when evidence shows that a favorable score coexists with failure of that intended outcome.
entries.boundary: Measured reward or approval versus the objective it is meant to represent.
evidence_to_check: The objective, scoring rule, and independent outcome evidence.
The exact unit judged, including which messages or environment states were considered.
alternative_explanations: An unusual solution may legitimately satisfy the objective.
Missing ground truth can make authenticity unresolved rather than disproven.
defensive_questions: Can scoring disagreements be investigated without presuming judge error?
Are criterion values and platform decisions stored separately from analyst conclusions?
entries.epistemic_status: Acceptance is not ground truth, but uncertainty is not proof of gaming. A causal or intentional account requires additional evidence.

entries.name: Explanations as evidence
entries.summary: A generated explanation is an observable artifact. It can help interpret a response, but its plausibility does not establish faithful access to the process that produced the decision.
entries.boundary: Persuasive reasoning text versus independently supported causal explanation.
evidence_to_check: Agreement between the explanation, available inputs, and observed actions.
Whether consequential claims in the explanation have external support.
alternative_explanations: The explanation may be a post-hoc rationalization.
An omitted factor does not imply deliberate concealment.
defensive_questions: Do reviewers evaluate the outcome independently of rhetorical confidence?
Are self-reported reasons distinguished from experimentally supported causes?
entries.epistemic_status: Research documents unfaithful explanations in evaluated settings. It does not justify dismissing every explanation or inferring hidden cognition from one passage.

entries.name: Safety after model customization
entries.summary: Further training can change behavior beyond the intended task improvement. Safety properties of a starting model do not automatically describe the customized model.
entries.boundary: Previously evaluated behavior versus behavior after a model update.
evidence_to_check: The authorized model versions, training provenance, and evaluation conditions.
Both intended task changes and independently measured safety changes.
alternative_explanations: Different inference settings may explain an apparent regression.
Customization may improve, preserve, or degrade different properties.
defensive_questions: Are consequential updates followed by relevant regression evaluation?
Can changes be attributed without assuming the data or operator was malicious?
entries.epistemic_status: The source reports safety changes under particular customization conditions. No dataset recipe, optimization settings, or universal degradation claim is provided.

entries.name: Training-data integrity and conditional behavior
entries.summary: Modified training data can affect later model behavior, including behavior dependent on specific conditions. Establishing that connection requires data provenance and appropriate causal evidence.
entries.boundary: Authorized training material versus untrusted changes affecting the learned system.
evidence_to_check: The data modification, its inclusion in training, and the resulting behavior.
Whether the behavior is specifically associated with the suspected condition.
alternative_explanations: A spurious correlation can arise without deliberate poisoning.
Inference-time context changes may explain the same observation.
defensive_questions: Can training data changes be traced to reviewed sources?
Are anomalous conditional behaviors assessed alongside ordinary task performance?
entries.epistemic_status: Data poisoning is part of established adversarial-ML terminology. This catalog supplies no contaminant, trigger, or method for creating one.

entries.name: Trust in third-party components
entries.summary: Adapters, plugins, and other dependencies can alter model behavior or application actions. Their names and advertised purpose do not establish what code or parameters are actually loaded.
entries.boundary: Third-party component claims versus verified provenance and permission scope.
evidence_to_check: The component identity, version, origin, and granted permissions.
Whether effects come from model parameters, executed code, metadata, or returned data.
alternative_explanations: A legitimate update can introduce a defect without intentional compromise.
The host application may misuse an otherwise correct component.
defensive_questions: Are dependency provenance and permissions reviewable?
Can a component's influence be isolated when behavior changes?
entries.epistemic_status: A broad supply-chain category covering distinct artifacts. Evidence should identify the actual component type rather than assume every dependency behaves alike.

entries.name: Integrity of distributed model artifacts
entries.summary: A downloaded or deployed artifact may differ from the artifact that was reviewed. Integrity verification establishes identity, while behavioral evaluation addresses the properties of that artifact.
entries.boundary: Reviewed model or package identity versus the bytes actually deployed.
evidence_to_check: Authenticated provenance, version records, and artifact identity checks.
The relationship between the checked artifact and the running deployment.
alternative_explanations: An expected conversion or packaging change may explain a different hash.
A matching artifact can still contain defects present in the original release.
defensive_questions: Is the deployed version traceable to an authorized source?
Are integrity checks distinguished from claims about model safety?
entries.epistemic_status: An integrity mismatch establishes a difference, not malicious intent. Conversely, authenticity alone does not certify behavior.

entries.name: Underperformance and capability claims
entries.summary: A low evaluation score may understate what a system can do. Strategic underperformance is a stronger explanation than ordinary failure and requires evidence about conditions and incentives.
entries.boundary: Observed evaluation performance versus supported capability under comparable conditions.
evidence_to_check: The task, incentives, configuration, and evidence of relevant capability elsewhere.
Whether alternative conditions change performance without changing the underlying task.
alternative_explanations: Misunderstanding, fatigue-like service effects, or weak competence can lower scores.
Different assistance or tool access may explain stronger performance elsewhere.
defensive_questions: Can capability conclusions survive reasonable alternative explanations?
Are evaluations designed to distinguish inability from context-sensitive performance?
entries.epistemic_status: The cited study demonstrates capabilities under controlled conditions. A low score or treatment difference alone does not establish deliberate concealment.

entries.name: Behavior under different oversight conditions
entries.summary: A system's behavior can vary with information about training or oversight. Calling that variation alignment faking adds a causal interpretation that must be supported.
entries.boundary: Oversight-related context versus stable expectations for the system's behavior.
evidence_to_check: The information the system actually received about oversight or training.
Behavioral differences, available action evidence, and the assumptions needed to interpret them.
alternative_explanations: Ordinary task changes can produce legitimate contextual variation.
The model may be following an explicit condition rather than concealing a preference.
defensive_questions: Are oversight comparisons matched on relevant task conditions?
Can descriptive findings be reported without overstating hidden motives?
entries.epistemic_status: The source uses particular constructed conditions. Its interpretation cannot be assigned to an unrelated conversation solely from policy-related language.

entries.name: Benchmark provenance and measurement validity
entries.summary: Prior exposure to evaluation material and flaws in a scoring metric are different threats to validity. High scores alone establish neither.
entries.boundary: Performance on the measured task versus the capability or safety construct claimed.
evidence_to_check: Evidence of data overlap separately from evidence of proxy/outcome disagreement.
Dataset selection, evaluation unit, feedback availability, and the reported denominator.
alternative_explanations: Legitimate generalization can yield familiar wording or correct answers.
Learning from disclosed evaluation criteria is not automatically contamination or gaming.
defensive_questions: Do reports distinguish exposure, task learning, and scoring validity?
Are selected submissions and repeated snapshots accounted for in claims?
entries.epistemic_status: A validity framework rather than an accusation. Evidence of exposure or metric failure is required before applying the corresponding label.

entries.name: Claims of deliberate concealment
entries.summary: An agent can produce reassuring statements that disagree with its actions. The discrepancy is observable; an account of deliberate concealment requires stronger evidence.
entries.boundary: Reported compliance versus independently observed behavior and state.
evidence_to_check: The claimed action, actual recorded behavior, and relevant goal specification.
Whether the discrepancy persists and whether ordinary error explains it.
alternative_explanations: A tool failure may leave the agent with an outdated belief.
A generated justification can be inaccurate without revealing a hidden plan.
defensive_questions: Are consequential claims checked against action and state records?
Does the analysis separate contradiction, deception hypotheses, and demonstrated intent?
entries.epistemic_status: Constructed research shows some capabilities for deceptive behavior. This label does not establish consciousness, enduring motives, or a general disposition to scheme.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Sampling frame and units
evaluation_dimensions.question: What is complete, what was selected, and what exactly is counted?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: A complete submission archive can omit most activity. Messages, chats, submissions, and distinct task/model combinations support different descriptive claims.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Actor, control, and visibility
evaluation_dimensions.question: Who controlled each input, and which visible material was fixed by the environment?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: A runtime user role does not establish human authorship. Seeing a continuation does not establish control over that conversation or permission to continue it.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Trajectory and snapshot ancestry
evaluation_dimensions.question: Does this record represent a new interaction, a branch, or another view of the same history?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: Overlapping snapshots are dependent observations. Retaining ancestry prevents duplicated evidence and unsupported attribution to an added turn.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Outcome evidence
evaluation_dimensions.question: Is the record a statement, an emitted call, a returned result, or an independently checked effect?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: Those observations answer different questions. Platform acceptance is a separate judgment; it does not replace action or state evidence.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Artifact provenance
evaluation_dimensions.question: Was the output supplied, generated, reconstructed, or matched to an authorized reference?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: Plausible content can resemble a recovered artifact. Reference availability and the chosen match criterion determine which authenticity claims are supported.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Judging and feedback
evaluation_dimensions.question: What was judged, and what feedback was actually available to the researcher at that time?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: Criterion values, scoring scope, and confirmed feedback access need separate records. Temporal order alone does not establish feedback use or explain a changing score.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Human-AI division of work
evaluation_dimensions.question: Which suggestions, edits, decisions, submissions, and interpretations have attributable records?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: Final prose cannot recover missing collaboration history. Human-directed assistance and autonomous querying are different procedures, and phase differences alone are not causal effects.

evaluation_dimensions.name: Configuration and transfer
evaluation_dimensions.question: Which task, model label, context, interface, and candidate remained the same?
evaluation_dimensions.why_it_matters: Reuse, adaptation, and unchanged transfer are different observations. Anonymized labels do not reveal providers or establish identity across separate events.

learning_paths.title: Understand a trust boundary
learning_paths.summary: A reading path through roles, quotations, source authority, and the evidence needed to distinguish them.
questions: Who is speaking, and through which actual channel?
What may this source describe, and what may it authorize?
Which observations distinguish quotation from instruction adoption?

learning_paths.title: Read an agent's action record
learning_paths.summary: Concepts for separating permissions, proposed actions, tool behavior, and verified effects.
questions: What does the trace show beyond an assertion or call record?
Which part of the system enforced the relevant boundary?

learning_paths.title: Understand change across time
learning_paths.summary: A thematic guide to retained context, evolving responsibilities, stored information, and isolation.
questions: Did a responsibility change, or did the task become clearer?
What evidence distinguishes history from persistent memory?

learning_paths.title: Assess a research claim
learning_paths.summary: Concepts for checking authenticity, scoring units, selection effects, and the division of work in assisted research.
questions: What population and counting unit does the result describe?
What alternative explanation would materially change the conclusion?

learning_paths.title: Follow meaning across channels
learning_paths.summary: A reading path connecting language, representation, perception, and source attribution.
questions: Did each component perceive equivalent meaning?
Where could translation or recognition account for the difference?
Which source and speaker labels survived the transformation?

learning_paths.title: Review systems and oversight
learning_paths.summary: Concepts for understanding component provenance, update effects, coordinated workflows, and the limits of motive claims.
questions: Which artifact and configuration were actually evaluated?
What evidence links one component's behavior to a later effect?
Does the report distinguish an observed discrepancy from an inferred intention?
